generic: Vitamin B3 (Niacin / Nicotinic acid and Nicotinamide)
pharm: Precursor of NAD/NADP coenzymes essential for cellular energy metabolism; in pharmacologic doses nicotinic acid lowers VLDL/LDL and triglycerides and raises HDL, while nicotinamide does not affect lipids.
quick: Nutrition (RDA): ~14-16 mg/day; pellagra: 50-100 mg several times daily; dyslipidemia (nicotinic acid): titrate to 1-2 g/day (max ~6 g)
Take with food and water; extended-release niacin at bedtime to reduce flushing
RDA amounts safe (~18 mg/day); high pharmacologic doses only if clearly needed
RDA amounts safe (~17 mg/day); avoid high lipid-lowering doses
Use high doses cautiously; nutritional doses generally safe
High-dose niacin can be hepatotoxic; contraindicated in significant hepatic disease
High dose: liver enzymes, fasting glucose, uric acid, lipid panel
summary: Vitamin B3 (niacin) exists as nicotinic acid and nicotinamide (niacinamide) and is a precursor of the coenzymes NAD and NADP that are central to energy metabolism. Nutritional doses prevent and treat pellagra (dermatitis, diarrhea, dementia). In large pharmacologic doses, nicotinic acid is an antidyslipidemic that lowers LDL cholesterol and triglycerides and raises HDL, but causes prostaglandin-mediated flushing and can cause hepatotoxicity, hyperglycemia, and hyperuricemia; nicotinamide shares the vitamin activity but lacks the lipid and flushing effects. This is a group/supplement entry summarizing both forms.
indications: Prevention and treatment of niacin deficiency (pellagra)
Dietary supplementation as a component of nutritional support
Adjunct to diet for severe hypertriglyceridemia and primary hyperlipidemia (high-dose nicotinic acid)

dosage.d: About 16 mg/day niacin equivalents for men and 14 mg/day for women
dosage.n: Higher in pregnancy (18 mg) and lactation (17 mg)

dosage.d: Nicotinamide 50-100 mg three to four times daily (commonly up to 300-500 mg/day)
Start 250-500 mg/day and titrate slowly to 1-2 g two to three times daily
Start 500 mg at bedtime; titrate by 500 mg every 4 weeks to 1-2 g at bedtime
dosage.n: Do not exceed 2 g/day; do not substitute IR and ER mg-for-mg

admin: Take with food and a full glass of water; do not take on an empty stomach
Take extended-release nicotinic acid at bedtime to limit daytime flushing
Pre-treating with aspirin 30 minutes before a dose and avoiding hot drinks/alcohol reduces flushing
Swallow extended-release tablets whole; do not crush or chew
Titrate high doses slowly to improve tolerability
moa: Niacin is converted in the body to nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD) and its phosphate (NADP), coenzymes required for numerous oxidation-reduction reactions in carbohydrate, fat, and protein metabolism and for cellular respiration. Deficiency impairs these pathways, producing pellagra. At pharmacologic doses nicotinic acid reduces hepatic synthesis of VLDL (and thus LDL) and lowers triglycerides, partly by inhibiting lipolysis in adipose tissue and reducing free fatty acid flux to the liver, while raising HDL cholesterol. The characteristic flushing is mediated by prostaglandin D2 release in the skin. Nicotinamide provides the vitamin (coenzyme) activity but does not have the lipid-lowering or vasodilatory (flushing) effects.

absolute: Active liver disease or unexplained persistent transaminase elevations (high-dose nicotinic acid)
relative: Diabetes mellitus or impaired glucose tolerance (hyperglycemia)
Unstable angina or acute MI phase

preg: At recommended dietary intakes niacin is required and safe in pregnancy (RDA about 18 mg/day). High pharmacologic (lipid-lowering) doses are not established as safe and should be used only if the potential benefit clearly justifies the risk.
lact: Niacin is a normal constituent of human milk; dietary-level intake (RDA about 17 mg/day during lactation) is safe. Avoid high lipid-lowering doses while breastfeeding unless clearly necessary.
renal: Nutritional doses are safe in renal impairment. High-dose nicotinic acid should be used cautiously because of altered drug handling and the potential for worsening hyperuricemia.
hepatic: High-dose nicotinic acid (especially sustained-release forms) can cause dose-related hepatotoxicity, including fulminant hepatic failure; it is contraindicated in active liver disease or unexplained persistent transaminase elevations. Monitor liver enzymes during high-dose therapy.

major: HMG-CoA reductase inhibitors (statins) - increased risk of myopathy/rhabdomyolysis when combined with high-dose niacin
moderate: Antihypertensives / vasodilators / nitrates - additive vasodilation and hypotension/flushing
Antidiabetic agents - niacin raises blood glucose and may require dose adjustment
Bile acid sequestrants - bind niacin; separate dosing by 4-6 hours
minor: Aspirin - reduces niacin flushing (a beneficial interaction)
interactions.food: Take with food to reduce GI upset; hot beverages can intensify flushing.
interactions.alcohol: Alcohol increases flushing and the risk of hepatotoxicity; avoid around dosing.
interactions.diagnostics: High doses may raise fasting glucose, uric acid, and transaminases; can cause false elevations in some urinary catecholamine and glucose tests.

monitoring: Liver function tests at baseline and during high-dose therapy
counsel: Flushing (warmth and redness, often of the face) is common with niacin and usually eases over weeks
Take an aspirin 30 minutes before your dose, take niacin with food, and avoid alcohol and hot drinks to reduce flushing
Take extended-release tablets at bedtime and swallow them whole
If you have diabetes or gout, your blood sugar or uric acid may rise - keep monitoring appointments
Report yellowing of the skin/eyes, dark urine, severe stomach pain, or muscle pain
pk: Lipid effects develop over weeks; flushing within minutes to an hour of immediate-release dosing
Immediate-release peaks ~30-60 minutes; extended-release peaks ~4-5 hours
Short; sustained lipid control requires regular dosing
Store at controlled room temperature; protect from moisture
pearls: Group/supplement entry: nicotinic acid (niacin) lowers lipids and causes flushing; nicotinamide (niacinamide) is the vitamin form WITHOUT lipid or flushing effects
Deficiency causes pellagra - the classic 'three Ds': dermatitis, diarrhea, dementia
Aspirin 30 minutes pre-dose, bedtime extended-release dosing, and food/alcohol avoidance minimize flushing
High-dose niacin can raise glucose and uric acid and is hepatotoxic - monitor LFTs, glucose, and urate; sustained-release forms are more hepatotoxic
Combining high-dose niacin with statins raises myopathy/rhabdomyolysis risk
missed: For supplementation, if you miss a dose take it when you remember; if it is almost time for the next dose, skip the missed one and resume your schedule - do not double up. For bedtime extended-release niacin, do not take a missed dose during the daytime; resume at the next bedtime.
overdose: Acute overdose of nicotinic acid causes intense flushing, itching, gastrointestinal upset, and hypotension; very large or chronic high doses can cause hepatotoxicity, hyperglycemia, and hyperuricemia. There is no specific antidote - manage with supportive care, fluids for hypotension, and monitoring of liver enzymes and glucose.
